Desolate
des'ō-lāt
adj. and v.t. (laid waste, forsaken; rendering Hebrew shamem, Greek eremos)
From Latin desolare, to leave alone — de, entirely, and solus, alone. Hebrew shamem carries both the ruin of a place and the horror of those who look at it; the same root gives the word rendered astonished.

Biblical Definition

Desolate means laid waste and left alone, and Hebrew joins the two ideas that English separates: shamem describes both the wasted land and the appalled onlooker. God warns Israel that even conquest must be gradual, lest the country empty out faster than it can be settled: “I will not drive them out from before thee in one year; lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee” (Exodus 23:29) — a mercy in the form of a delay. Jeremiah pronounces the sentence on Judah with a limit attached: “The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end” (Jeremiah 4:27), the clause on which the whole doctrine of the remnant hangs. Ezekiel says the same to Edom without that clause: “I will lay thy cities waste, and thou shalt be desolate” (Ezekiel 35:4). And the word describes a man as well as a country. Lamentations 3:11 is one of the loneliest sentences in Scripture: “He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces: he hath made me desolate” — written by a man who, twelve verses later, says the LORD's mercies are new every morning.

Webster 1828 Definition

Laid waste; forsaken; left alone. The Hebrew word covers both the ruined place and the horror of those who behold it. Jeremiah's sentence on Judah carries the clause on which the remnant doctrine hangs: yet will I not make a full end.

expand to see more

DESOLATE, a. [L. desolatus; de and solus, alone.] Destitute of inhabitants; laid waste; ruined.

2. Solitary; without a companion; afflicted; as, a desolate widow.

3. DESOLATE, v.t. To lay waste; to ruin; to deprive of inhabitants.

4. DESOLATION, n. Destruction; ruin; a place laid waste; also, gloominess of mind.

5. In Scripture, The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end, Jer. 4; he hath made me desolate, Lam. 3.

Key Scripture

Exodus 23:29 — "I will not drive them out from before thee in one year; lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee."

Jeremiah 4:27 — "For thus hath the LORD said, The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end."

Lamentations 3:11 — "He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces: he hath made me desolate."

Ezekiel 35:4 — "I will lay thy cities waste, and thou shalt be desolate, and thou shalt know that I am the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Judgment in Scripture is almost never total, and the qualifying clauses are regularly overlooked by readers on both sides — by those who find the prophets merely vindictive, and by those who preach ruin without the remnant.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the doctrine of the remnant. Jeremiah's sentence is severe and its qualification is deliberate: the whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end. Isaiah says that except the LORD of hosts had left a very small remnant, Israel would have been as Sodom; Paul takes up the same word to describe his own generation — even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. God has never once left Himself without a witness, and He has usually left fewer than anyone expected and more than anyone could see.

Lamentations 3 shows what this means for a person rather than a nation, and it is worth reading in order. The man who writes he hath made me desolate has already said that God has broken his bones, walled him about, and filled him with bitterness; he is not managing his feelings. And then, without retracting a word of it, he says: This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. The hope is not a denial of the desolation. It is recalled deliberately, in the middle of it, which is the only place such hope is ever needed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shamem means both to be laid waste and to be appalled; shemamah is a wasteland. Greek eremos is desert or deserted, and eremosis gives the abomination of desolation.

expand to see more

Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, to be appalled; one root for the ruin and for the horror at it.

Hebrew shemamah (H8077) — a wasteland or desolation; the state of a land emptied of inhabitants.

Hebrew she'ar (H7605) — a remnant, that which is left; the qualification on nearly every sentence of ruin.

Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, solitary, deserted; used of the wilderness and of a house left desolate.

Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; the noun in the abomination of desolation.

Usage

"Of a conquest slowed in mercy: lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee (Exodus 23:29)."

"Of judgment with the remnant clause attached: The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end (Jeremiah 4:27)."

"Of a man's own condition under affliction: he hath made me desolate (Lamentations 3:11)."
